name: Funeral March
title: Chopin's Funeral March
alsoKnownAs: Funeral March from Piano Sonata No. 2, Op. 35
about: Frédéric Chopin wrote his Funeral March in 1837 and made it the slow third movement of his Piano Sonata No. 2 in B flat minor, Op. 35, published in 1840. It was played at Chopin's own funeral in Paris in 1849, and its opening, one low note tolling in a slow dotted rhythm like a bell, has been the sound of a funeral procession ever since, in concert halls, cartoons and haunted houses alike.

This is the march's opening theme, its first ten bars, read from Jan Kleczyński's Warsaw edition of the march and checked against a St. Louis printing of 1897: the tolling B flats, the turn down from D flat, the same again a third higher, and the answer that falls from the B flat above before the bell comes back. The piano plays it in chords over a rocking bass; this page has the tune alone, and the grace notes are left out.
confidence: hand-encoded from a public-domain score, unchecked
licence: Public domain. Chopin died in 1849 and Jan Kleczyński, who edited the Warsaw edition the tune is read from, in 1895; the score scanned is Gebethner & Wolff's edition, digitised by the Jagiellonian Library (Kraków), which marks it public domain, at the Internet Archive.
credits: Melody read from the Marche funèbre, Op. 35, in Jan Kleczyński's edition of Chopin's works (Warsaw: Gebethner & Wolff), the Jagiellonian Library's copy at the Internet Archive, checked against Spang & Luhn's St. Louis edition (1897); public domain.
reviewNotes: Hand-encoded from Kleczyński's edition (Gebethner & Wolff, Internet Archive jbc.bj.uj.edu.pl.NDIGMUZ024770: PDF page 5, music page 3, the first two systems): bars 1–10, read off a 400 dpi render, and checked note for note and beat for beat against Spang & Luhn's edition (St. Louis, 1897, Internet Archive b10312481, page [3]), which agrees. In bars 1–3 and 9 the tune is the top note of the right hand's chords, printed on the bass staff (the B flat below middle C); from the last beat of bar 3 it is on the treble staff. Bar 4 is printed C. B♭ B♭. B♭ | B♭ in both editions (the semiquaver is B flat, not A). Bars 5–6 are the top of the right hand's thirds; bars 7 and 8 are the same. Left out: the grace notes (F before bar 6, A flat before the G flat of bars 7 and 8, D flat before bar 10, and in Spang & Luhn only one before the C of bar 4), the chords, the bass and the staccato dots. Bars 9–10 repeat bars 3–4: the page stops at the B flat that closes the first strain, before the forte phrase of bar 11. Tempo 54 is ours: neither edition prints a tempo mark. Dates: 1837 (written) and 1840 (the sonata first published) are the commonly given ones; check them. The edition's date (c. 1890) is the Jagiellonian Library's.
